inline.s: Bai Guinian. He obtained a wondrous book, and could understand the speech of the birds of the nine heavens and the tongues of the beasts of the nine earths. One day he was sitting with the prefect of Luzhou when a flock of sheep was driven past below the courtyard. Among them was one sheep that would not go on under the whip, and bleated mournfully. The prefect said: What is the sheep saying? Bai said: The sheep says there is a lamb in her belly. When she has given birth, she will gladly go to death. The prefect then kept the sheep and did not kill it. In time she bore two lambs.

Wen Li. His trade was cooking and butchery. He once killed a deer. The deer knelt and wept, which he took for an ill omen. The deer was with young, and the time of its birthing was near. It came to the kitchen in utter grief, and was cut open all the same. Afterwards he suffered a strange disease: his hair fell out and his skin rotted. Then a deep remorse arose in him. He emptied his household to buy land and built the Little Adornment Temple. His illness was cured, and he cultivated practice to the end of his life. To rip open a womb and kill the unborn is the gravest of crimes. Yet there is a way of mending one's faults. Consider this case.

The Buddha said: If a man be violent and wicked, not believing in guilt and blessing, and catches fledglings and eats eggs, causing the birds each to lose their young, so that they cry out in grief till the blood starts from their eyes, he shall reap the retribution of being solitary and childless.

Yang Xu dreamed that a god said to him: In ten days you shall die. If you can save countless lives, you may be spared. Xu protested that the time was too short to suffice. The god said: The Buddha taught that fish roe, if not soaked in salt, may yet come to life again after three years. Xu woke, and daily bought fish with roe and released them, and wrote the god's words in large characters on the highways, so that people who saw them knew to take heed. When he saw a man kill a fish, he took the roe and cast it into the river. After some days he dreamed again that the god said: The number of countless lives is complete. Your span may be extended. Here is appended Master Shi Yushan's method for releasing fish roe. When a fish is already dead, gently take out the roe; do not bruise it, and do not let it touch salt water. Spread it on a bundle of rice straw, and when the water has somewhat dried, bury it shallowly in the sand and mud at the water's edge, so that it escapes being swallowed by fish and comes to live. But the burying place must not be far from the water. Another method: wrap the roe in dry mud, dry it in the sun, and store it warm. From the end of winter through the three months of spring, gather it until after the fifteenth of the fourth month, then release it among the water plants on the riverbank, and all will live. In other months it may be released at any time. This is especially convenient.
Zhou Yu once boiled eels, and saw one that bowed its body upright, dipping head and tail into the boiling water. It was because there were young in its belly. From this he gave up killing.

In the reign of Emperor Wenzong of Tang, the imperial kitchen, preparing food for the table, was boiling hen's eggs when suddenly there came a faint sound from the cauldron: a chorus crying out, Guanshiyin Bodhisattva, most pitiful and bitter. The kitchen overseer reported it, and the emperor sent men to verify it, and so it was. The emperor sighed and said: I did not know the power of the Buddha's way could be like this. Thereupon he decreed that from that day no hen's eggs be used. To save the suffering and rescue the distressed is the original practice of Guanshiyin. If a flock of them could cry out from within a cauldron, how much more should a human being revere and invoke her.

In the Liang dynasty there was a man who washed his hair with egg white mixed with water, wishing to make it so glossy that it might serve as a mirror. He broke a very great many eggs. As he lay dying, from among his hair came the sound of several thousand chicks chirping.

Hu Jiadong said: The flying and running of creatures is as the walking of men. The hibernating and perching of creatures is as the resting of men. The nests and dens of creatures are as the palaces and houses of men. The wombs and eggs of creatures are as the pregnancy of men. How can one maim and kill them in every fashion, cutting off the compassion of Heaven and Earth's creative working, and turning aside from the benevolence that sees all things as one body? Yet these eight kinds of harm are everywhere present, and one cannot hope that they will all cease at once. I would only exhort people everywhere: those who have wealth should make releasing life their chief work; those who have none should, beyond abstaining from killing themselves, also kindly persuade their kin, neighbors, and friends to create no more evil. If this method spreads, perhaps there may be some relief.

Master Lianchi of the Ming, in his Essay on Releasing Life, says: I have heard that of all things in the world, life is the most precious, and of all deeds under heaven, killing and wounding are the most cruel. Therefore when the hand reaches for them they flee; even fleas and lice know to shun death. When rain is coming they move away; even ants and crickets still crave life. How is it, then, that men net them on the mountains and snare them in the deeps, masking their taking in a hundred ways; curve the hook and straighten the arrow, searching them out by a hundred schemes, till their gall bursts and their soul flies, the mother parted from her young and the young scattered? Some are caged and penned, as in a prison; some are laid on the block, as at an execution. The deer that pities its fawn licks its wounds and its tender bowels are cut inch by inch. The ape that fears death, seeing the shadow of the bow, lets fall two streams of bitter tears. To rely on my strength and oppress their weakness — surely this is not right. To eat another's flesh to nourish my own body — how can the heart bear it? Therefore Heaven above took pity and the sages of old practiced benevolence. The opening of the net was set forth by Tang the Completer; the keeping of fish was begun by Zichan. Holy was the Flowing Water, who saved the parched with a sack of spring water. Compassionate was Shakyamuni, who gave his flesh in place of the doomed. The Wise One of Tiantai dug pools for releasing life; the Great Tree Immortal protected the birds that nested in him. Ransoming scales and shells and thereby gaining deliverance — the lingering love of Chan Master Yongming still remains. Saving the dragon's son and handing down the method — the kindly spirit of Master Sun the True Man is not yet lost. Once, for saving an ant, a novice monk exchanged a short life for a long one. Once, a scholar who released a turtle exchanged a lowly name for the highest place. Once, for releasing a turtle, Mao Bao escaped peril in his extremity, and Kong Yu by a petty office was enfeoffed as a marquis. Master Qu released a carp at Yuancun and gained twelve more years. The Marquis of Sui saved a snake in the fields of Qi and a pearl repaid him a thousand in gold. He rescued a fly already drowning, and the death sentence of the vintner was remitted. He let go a turtle about to be cooked, and the kitchen maid's grave illness was healed. Trading a doomed life away from the butcher's house, Inspector Zhang's soul rose to the heavens. Buying back a life from the fishing boat, Li Jingwen's cinnabar poison was dissolved. Sun Liangsi freed birds from the peril of the snare, and when he divined for a burying place the feathered creatures came to help him. Magistrate Pan set prohibitions for rivers and lakes, and when he left office the water tribes wailed in grief. Elder Xin spared the beasts of the foolish villagers, and Xiangfu had sweet rain. Caoxi guarded the hunter's net, and his Way spread through the divine land. The sparrow that unclasped the ring repaid the kindness; the fox could teach a craft beside the well. Even to the maimed body that gained life, the white wall was hung and the sutra heard; in a place of hardship it sought to live, and appeared in yellow robes in a dream. Giving is always repaid; these things are not without proof. They are recorded in the books and shine before eyes and ears. I pray that all may, according to whatever creature they see, rouse a compassionate heart, give away wealth that does not endure, and do the deeds of skillful means. Or if the kindness reaches many lives, then great hidden merit is accumulated. Even if the benefit touches but one insect, how is that not a good deed? If day by day it increases and month by month it accumulates, of itself it will broaden and blessing will rise. Compassion fills the human realm, and the name reaches the heavenly palace. Clearing away the hindrances of resentment, many blessings gather in this life. Watering and steeping the roots of goodness, the surplus blessing reaches other lives. If one further helps by intoning the Buddha's name and adds the recitation of sutras, dedicating the merit to the West, causing those beings forever to leave the evil paths, then the intent is greater still and the planted virtue deeper. The work of the Way will be aided to swift completion, and the lotus terrace will bring forth a surpassing grade.

When a man has a fault, it is his misfortune. Not to pity him but instead to wish him ill is to take pleasure in his calamity. Since he takes calamity and disaster as things to rejoice and be glad in, how can calamity and disaster fail to follow after him? So the fault is not in the other man but in oneself. A man, however foolish, should not do this.

Li Shiheng was sent as envoy to Korea, with Yu Ying as his deputy. All the gifts of silk they received were entrusted to Ying. Ying, afraid that the crossing of the sea might wet them, put all of Heng's goods at the bottom of the boat and his own on top. Unexpectedly they met a great wind, and the boatmen begged to lighten the load. In the confusion they threw things overboard at random. When the wind settled and they checked what had been cast away, all of it was Ying's goods. Heng's goods, being at the bottom, were not lost at all. Such private calculations — who does not have them? It all comes of being unable to regard things equally. The Nirvana Sutra says: All practitioners should use the six dharmas of the power of equal wisdom to govern their own minds, so that in every application all is equal. Shao Kangjie's poem says: Each day at dawn a stick of incense, thanking Heaven, thanking Earth, thanking the sovereign. I ask only that the grain ripen everywhere, and wish only that all men's years be long. May the state have worthy ministers to keep the altars of soil and grain at peace, and the home have no rebellious son to vex father and mother. May the four quarters be quiet and the spears and shields be still; and though I be poor, it is no harm. From this we know that the heart of the three teachings is one: it all comes from equality. We should keep this measure in our hearts, restrain ourselves, and govern our minds, and not by thought after thought of selfishness create layer upon layer of evil.

To destroy has two senses: one is to break down, the other is to slander. When a man wishes to accomplish a work, great or small, there is none but strives with all his might to bring it to completion. Yet if I must thwart, obstruct, and ruin it, then my mind is truly that of a serpent or scorpion. Zhen Xishan of the Song said: When a man hears of one good thing in another, he should praise and second it; when he hears of sundry evils, he must strive to cover them, so that the man may succeed and not fail in virtue. Thus did the ancients keep their minds. How much less should one destroy what is already accomplished?

Zeng Xian of the Ming was governor-general of the three frontier regions and wished to recover the great river bend. Yan Song envied his success and instead slandered Zeng Xian and Xia Yan for provoking border conflict of their own accord. Both were executed at the Western Market. Later Yan Song's property was confiscated, and his son Shifan was beheaded and his head hung up.

Xuan Qiying of the Song was of a dangerous nature. A neighbor was building a house and it was nearly finished; Xuan envied him, and went by night to cut through the base of his pillars. Suddenly the beam fell and crushed him to death. Alas. He who destroys others destroys only himself. People today, in some matter or some thing — even in trade and lending and the like — will often use a single word to ruin another's success. What manner of heart is that? I know that they only destroy themselves. Let all us good people take heed together.

The thousand sutras and ten thousand scriptures speak of nothing but the one word, mind. Now when a man shares calamity and trouble with others and yet wishes to make others bear the danger while he himself dwells in safety, he has already lost his original mind. Yu Tieqiao said: To leave danger and take safety is the common way of human feeling. Why then does Heaven hate it? Not because it hates a man's seeking his own safety, but because it hates his endangering others. In every situation a man passes through there is a division between safety and danger. If he knows only how to make himself safe and pays no heed to endangering others, then the killing intent lurks within and he may stop at nothing. If his schemes were allowed to succeed, then the cunning would all sleep on high pillows and the simple would be left without a single survivor. Is that the mind of Heaven and Earth? Moreover the chances of safety and danger turn like a ring, and in the end they do not suffer a selfish man to see through them. Hence it happens that what he hastens toward is instead a perilous place, and what he avoids is instead level ground. If only he would calm his mind between self and other, then wherever he goes would be solid rock.

Li Xu of the Song was magistrate of Yong'an Army. At that time great bandits were rising, and he feared disaster would reach him. So he cunningly recommended his friend Fan Xing to take his place. Thereupon Xing became magistrate of Yong'an, and Xu was able to leave his post. Later Xing's whole household was destroyed by the bandits. Before long Xu went to Lin'an for reassignment, met bandits on the road, and his whole family died as well. Alas. When a gentleman sees another in danger, he thinks only of saving him. How could he bear to endanger others for his own safety? This is the deed of a mean and heartless petty man, and it brings the greatest calamity.

In all the world, only he who benefits others can truly benefit himself. If a thing does not benefit others but benefits oneself, it is still not true benefit. How much worse, then, to diminish others and take abundance for oneself! This is what is meant by caring only that oneself be rich and not that others be poor. Yu Tieqiao said: People today in matters of money and silk, land and houses, do this often. Do they not know that this is merely borrowing without drawing up a bond? The interest will grow day by day, and the term will come due day by day. What benefit is there in it?

At the beginning of the Chongzhen reign of the Ming, two scholars, A and B, were on friendly terms. When the military examination came, each recommended one military candidate: A through the county magistrate, B through the judicial officer, each owing a fee of fifty pieces of gold. A judged that the county magistrate's influence was light and he would surely fail, while the judicial officer's influence was weighty and the matter would surely succeed. So he wished to diminish B to benefit himself, and devised a scheme, saying to B: You and I are of one mind and should share sweet and bitter alike. If only one of them is enrolled, then, whoever it be, let us divide the fee equally. B agreed. When the results were posted, the one recommended through the judicial officer was in fact left out, while the one recommended through the county magistrate was enrolled. The sealed fee for the other was all in B's keeping. A could not go back on his word, and could only mope. Now A wished to benefit himself and instead benefited another. Extending this, all officials who fleece the people and rich houses that hoard interest, thinking to fill their purses and fatten themselves, never fail to be the ones who instead suffer loss.

To exchange evil for good, as iron for gold, stone for jade, cotton for silk, and the like: such a deed is not enough to draw a smile from a broad-minded man, yet the mind behind it is close to theft. The Fourth Patriarch said: Circumstances and conditions have no beauty or ugliness; beauty and ugliness arise from the mind. If the mind does not force names upon things, whence do false feelings arise? Master Wonhyo of Donghai came to the land of Tang seeking a teacher, and one night lodged among the wild graves. Being thirsty, he longed for a drink, and beside where he sat saw a small pool of water. Scooping it up, he drank, and it was very sweet. At dawn he looked: it was the liquid of a corpse. Then his mind loathed it and he vomited. Thereupon he was suddenly and greatly enlightened, and said: The three realms are mind only; the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness only. Beauty and ugliness are from myself — what has it to do with the water?

Su Dongpo of the Song treasured a fine piece of jade. There was one Zhang Chi who asked to see it, and secretly exchanged it for a swallow-stone. Dongpo did not notice. On reaching Huangzhou he opened it and looked, and only then knew that Zhang Chi had exchanged it. He merely smiled. Before long Zhang Chi died in exile at Taizhou. Who knows into whose hands the fine jade has passed.

Private is spoken of with respect to the mind; public is spoken of with respect to principle. When by the likes and dislikes, the favors and grudges of private intent one sets aside the right and wrong, the crooked and straight, of public principle, then above, where loyalty and flattery are not distinguished, the court suffers the calamity of factional collusion; and below, where the wicked and the upright are not examined, friends and fellow villagers fall under the suspicion of banding with their own and attacking those who differ. Going further, when love and hatred are not rightly placed, then even family members, father and son, the nearest flesh and blood, become a gathering place of resentment. Of the obscurations of human feeling, none is greater than this. Whether worthy or foolish, noble or base, everyone sits in this sickness; only some are worse and some less. He who knows this obscuration examines principle to melt away the nature of partial attachment, and calms his mind to dissolve the views of a guarded heart. Such a one is a man of great learning and great capacity.

Zhao Bian and Fan Zhen of the Song had a rift because of a dispute over policy. When Wang Anshi became minister, he hated Fan Zhen for his accusing memorials, and taking advantage of the emperor's asking about Zhen, he said: Zhao Bian knows what manner of man he is. The emperor asked Bian, and Bian said: He is a loyal minister. The emperor said: How do you know he is loyal? Bian said: When Emperor Renzong was ill, Zhen was the first to petition for the establishment of an heir to the throne to settle the altars of soil and grain. He submitted nineteen memorials, waited a hundred days for the decree, and his beard and hair turned white. If he is not a loyal minister, what is he? After he withdrew, Anshi reproached him: Have you not a rift with him? Bian said: How dare I set aside public principle for a private rift?

Kong Yi, magistrate of Luoyang, set a fire in front of his hall. Every letter of solicitation that came he threw into the fire, saying: A county magistrate is closest to the people, and on the path of office there are many who seek favors. To grant them is for the people to suffer harm; to refuse is unavoidably to invite blame. So if a letter comes and I do not open it, but throw it straight into the fire, then on my side I do not know what the matter is, and on theirs they are not offended. Right and wrong follow the people, and impartial judgment has its law. How could I set these aside for private ends? Later one of his sons became a metropolitan graduate at nineteen.

Yang Sizhong was skilled in geomancy, and chose a very fine site for a man of high position. Just as he was marking the grave's eye, a sudden rain came down from the mountain. That night he dreamed that a god said: Do not give this land to him. This man, as an examination official, sold three candidates. He is due for hidden calamity; to give him the land would be to defy Heaven's intent. Sizhong awoke and made an excuse to go home. Not long after, because of a dispute over land he was entangled in a lawsuit, and before the burial took place his family declined into poverty.

To steal means to take what is not one's own. To steal another's writing and make it one's own; to steal another's plan and make it one's own devising; to steal another's achievement and make it one's own accomplishment; to steal a teacher's instruction and make it one's own insight — all these are deeds of deceiving oneself and deceiving others. Condemnation is certain.

When Mount Liang collapsed, the lord of Jin summoned the great officer Bo Zong. On the road he met a cart-puller and asked him: Have you heard anything? The man said: Mount Liang has collapsed and blocked the river so that it does not flow. The great officer Bo Zong is summoned. Bo Zong said: What is to be done? The man said: Let the lord lead his ministers and weep over it, and afterwards sacrifice to it, and the river will flow. Bo Zong reported his words to the lord, and the river flowed. The lord of Jin asked Bo Zong: How did you know? Bo Zong answered that he had known it himself. Confucius heard of it and said: Bo Zong will have no descendants, I fear. He seized another man's good deed. Afterwards Bo Zong indeed met with murder, and his ministerial rank came to an end. If stealing a single word from another man brings condemnation like this, then how much more for the greater cases.

To obscure means to cover, so that a thing is not exposed. The Buddhist scriptures say: The single word good is the most able to bring to fulfillment all the vows and practices of people in the world. Therefore when a man has one word or one deed of goodness, it should be proclaimed and made known, with fear only that it cannot be made bright enough. Then not only does it complete that man's fair name, but it can also stir others' good thoughts. Passed on from one to another, such encouragement raises up a great many. It is a joyful thing. Why then obscure it? He who obscures it must have no least fondness for goodness in his heart, and must harbor the thought of envy besides. Therefore he does not wish another's excellence to be seen, lest it throw his own evil into relief. Such a man is the inauspicious man of the world.

Chen Shou of the Jin wrote the Record of the Three Kingdoms. He said to Ding Liangzhou: If you lend me a thousand measures of rice, I will write a fine biography of your honored father. Liangzhou did not respond to his request, and so he wrote no biography. When the history appeared, men mocked him together. Chen Shou afterwards met with murder.

Two scholars of Jiangyin were compiling the county gazetteer. They happened upon the affairs of two chaste wives, plain and unremarkable, and struck them out. The Taoist priest of the City God's temple at night heard two women weeping and complaining, saying: We endured a lifetime of bitter chastity, and at our death were recorded in the county gazetteer. Now for no cause we have been struck out by men. The god said: These two scholars are due to ascend the yellow roster. Since they have obscured men's chastity and righteousness, their emoluments shall be cut away. The two women wept, bowed, and departed. The two scholars heard of it and denounced it as nonsense. The next year they indeed failed in the inferior grade of examination and lost their stipends. Both died of pent-up fury.

A man's ugly conduct is what is called something shameful to speak of and unfit for others to hear. Yet if you describe and expose it, then your own generous way is wounded, and your hidden merit is forfeited along with it. The Recorded Sayings of Panshan says: For a practitioner it is a great taboo to speak of others' right and wrong, beauty and ugliness, or indeed of any affair of the world that does not concern oneself. The mouth must not speak of it, the mind must not think of it. For the mouth to speak and the mind to think is to be blind to oneself. If one devotes oneself to refining the mind and constantly searches out one's own faults, what leisure is there to mind the affairs in another man's house? Grind the bones to powder and shatter the body, and let only the mind not move. Gather in one's own mind, and at every hour and moment investigate the true place of one's own original nature. From this we see that a man should make governing himself his urgent task, and at every thought fear lest his own body and mind be at fault. What leisure has he to mind others?

When Liu Zhongfu was newly married, a thief came into his room. He looked up in alarm and saw it was an acquaintance. He said: Are you poor? He took out two head ornaments and gave them to him, and added: I will never speak of it. Do not offend again. Then he let him go. Afterwards his wife asked the man's name, and he said: I have promised not to speak. Why ask about it? When he died, there was a man who had formerly been a rogue and afterwards became a doer of good, who wore sackcloth and mourning and wept most bitterly. The family suspected he was the thief of former days. His grandson Sun Sui became a minister, with the posthumous title Zhuangxiang.

A physiognomist told Xi Kuang that in a certain year he would die. Kuang was greatly troubled. By chance he came upon men talking of the affairs of the women's quarters, and as Kuang faced them his countenance flushed with anger. The talkers, ashamed at heart, stopped. And so the matter was hidden. In the year named he was in fact unharmed. Later he rose to the rank of chief minister. The ancients said: If in a whole gathering there is one who shoots at others with words, I alone sit upright and silent, and so dissolve it. This is the teaching without words. A man like Lord Xi may serve as a model.

Nie Congyi loved to mock. When a man had ugly conduct, he would be sure to set it out in poems, rhapsodies, songs, and ballads, so that it spread far and could not be hidden. He even broke up men's marriages, disgraced men's women's quarters, and separated men from their kin. Afterwards he was implicated in a matter and died in exile at Dengzhou. Alas. For the crime of exposing ugliness, other cases might still be forgiven; but the one matter of the women's quarters weighs especially heavy. Mockery and rumor, the dog barking at a shadow — I have already made the cause of the pulled-out tongue, and the other still bears a lifelong shame. Flesh and blood are maimed, sons and grandsons bear the filth. The matter is no small one, and the great evil is hard to transcend.

Zheng Xuan was of a quiet and reserved nature. He once said: In a crowd or a great gathering, one must not give free rein to talk and argument. It not only invites envy but also wounds others. Is there never one who is ugly among them? When the talk reaches him, then he says nothing but resents it in his heart. If you speak of purity before an official, the impure are angered; if you speak of uprightness before a friend, the crooked hate you. They will say I did it on purpose. There is nothing for it but to be sparing of words, mild of countenance, and to answer only what is asked. Perhaps then it may be well. These words have deeply grasped the way of dealing with the world, and so I append them here.

To point out and attack means to accuse. Private things are matters dark and unlit. A man is not a sage or a worthy; who has no hidden private matters? I ought not to go looking for them. If I peer into the leaks of his house and broadcast them in the great hall, leaving him no place to stand, that is the most dangerous and poisonous of deeds. Heaven is angered and men resent it, and the calamity sown is no small one. Take heed, take heed.

When Su Song was in Hangzhou, a man asked him to do something for him privately. Su Song would not consent, and the man afterwards became a censorial official and, nursing his anger, slandered him. Someone urged Su Song to submit the letter of former days. Su Song said: To accuse a man of his private matters — would I do such a thing? The True Man Xujing said: As for covering faults and hiding wrongs, one must not have this in oneself, but one must not be without it toward others. For if one shields oneself, goodness cannot enter; but to shield others is a deed of abundant virtue.

In the court of Empress Wu of the Tang, slaughter was forbidden. Zhang De the Reminder had a son born, and privately killed a sheep to feast his colleagues. Du Su wrapped up some of the meat and accused him of it in a memorial. The next day the empress said to Zhang De: I hear with great joy that you have a son. Zhang De bowed and thanked her. The empress said: Where did you get the meat? Zhang De knocked his head on the ground and confessed his crime. The empress said: I forbade slaughter, but auspicious and inauspicious occasions are not included. From now on, when you invite guests, you must also choose your man. She brought out Du Su's memorial and showed it to him. Du Su was deeply ashamed, and the whole court wished to spit in his face. Du Su afterwards fell into ruin.

Dao Gai of the Liang: his grandfather Yanzhi had once carried night soil to keep himself alive. When Gai was in charge of the Ministry of Personnel, He Jingrong made a request that was not granted, and so he said to others: Dao Gai still has the stench about him, and now he learns to play the great man. Gai heard of it and hated him deeply. Gai's younger brother Qia one day asked Liu Xiaochuo: I greatly wish to buy the land of my eastern neighbor, but its owner makes difficulties. What is to be done? Xiaochuo said: Only cart a great deal of night soil beside it to make him miserable, and he will move away. Qia was angry, and in the end ruined him by some affair. Alas. One word wounds the harmony of Heaven and Earth; one deed brews a lifetime's calamity. Therefore in dealing with the world we must not use heated words and jesting speech, causing a man's resentment to sink into his marrow. The proverb says: In striking a man, do not strike his knee; in speaking of a man, do not speak the truth of him. How telling.

This refers to that class of wicked and evil petty men who delude the foolish and infatuated, luring them into whoring, gambling, litigation, and alchemical refining, while they themselves profit in the midst of it. Unworthy sons and younger brothers, fooled by them, pay no regard to the toil by which father and grandfather founded the household, and in a single morning squander it all, losing the family and their own lives. Tracing it to its source, whose fault is it? Can they escape evil retribution?

Wen Qi was a man of Shu who plied the art of alchemical refining, and all the nobles were deceived by him. The rich merchant Li Shiwu was deluded by Wen Qi's art, and in three years his household was ruined and he hanged himself. Wen Qi went on to Jianzhou and rented a house to refine his elixir. By chance a fire broke out and burned a whole district. Wen Qi fled into the mountains and was driven out by fierce beasts. He was seized and sent to the officials, and according to the law was sentenced to beheading.

Xu Chi of the Ming was rich and violent. He wished to obtain Xu Ba's house, and so had men entice Ba's son into whoring and dissipation, until his debts piled up, and he got the house. Afterwards his two sons and five grandsons all contracted illness. The shaman said Xu Ba was working mischief. Chi was afraid, and held a rite of purification, seeking release at the City God's temple. A beggar came up and asked him: Are you not Xu Chi? Last night I slept in a secluded spot in the temple, and there was one who called your name before the god. You harmed him, and the god too was greatly angered. Chi fled in terror and died. His sons and grandsons had not a single survivor. Now the brothel is the karmic cause of debt-repayment, and the painted beauty is truly the sea of evil that wrecks a house. People today all know this. Yet once the foul flesh is joined, sores and poisons break out, the five senses are displaced, and calamity flows through three generations. Still those who know it try it on their own bodies and do not avoid it. Why?

A certain Qian of Wuxi gathered a gang of more than ten and lured the sons of rich families, then used loaded dice to throw for them. In gambling he always won. Later he played a match with a young man and won as much as several hundred thousand. Suddenly all the dice flew out of the basin, and Qian fell to the ground, blood pouring from mouth and nose, and died. At the time a Taoist was invoking the planchette, and Lord Guan descended with a revelation: at a certain place he would rid the world of a villain, and he instructed that three dice be placed on the beam of that house. The Taoist followed and came to the house, where he found the group gathered in astonishment. He had a ladder brought and looked above, and found them. Then he related in full the words of Lord Guan. The wicked company was greatly alarmed, and one after another died of plague. Again, Ding Shi: a physiognomist promised him first place in the whole realm. Later he met the physiognomist again, who cried out in shock: What have you done? It has been taken from you. Ding reflected that he had once performed a rite to delay [fate] and gambled and won six million. So he told the truth. The physiognomist said: That is it. Ding greatly repented, and hurried to return his winnings to atone. In the end he only came in at the tail of the list. Now those who commit this offense are everywhere. Yet the country gentry and scholars relish it above all, which is the more hateful. The saying goes: A licentiate is like a maiden — he must fear others. A metropolitan graduate is like a daughter-in-law — he must nourish others. In retirement he is like a grandmother — he must teach others. Those men cannot nourish or teach others, and that is the end of it; yet they further wish to harm other men's sons and younger brothers. What manner of heart is that?

Mao Qizong of the Ming was a man of Rugao in Jiangsu. He once wrote warning words, saying: I have often seen that in the houses of the powerful and noble and in the mansions of the rich, unworthy sons and grandsons are lewd and dissipated and give themselves up to extravagance. Some, before the man is dead, have secretly sold the property to another house; some, before the flesh is cold, have had men divide and seize his rooms. What former generations piled up by the inch and the quarter, later generations cast away like mud and sand. And those unworthy ones are for the most part clever men. Why is this so? It is because in former days they put forth their might and wielded their cunning, coercing and ensnaring, wasting countless others to make up one rich house of their own. First they wasted others; afterwards they were wasted by others. The saying goes: What came by unclear means goes by the same road. This is what it means. From this we see that those who are wasted today are the ones who wasted others in former days. Then can those who waste others today fail, before another turn of the eye, to be wasted by others in their turn?
Appended: Ten Rules Against Gambling.

First, it ruins the mind. Once a man enters the gambling house, it becomes a thicket of profit. He calculates by a hundred schemes, and it is all one mass of greed. The two parties plot each other's downfall and give rise to endless evil thoughts. Even when closest kin play a match, they secretly set spear and halberd against each other; even when good friends share the same table, they are as solemn as enemies. Each cares only that he himself win money; who cares that another is ruined? Is the mind not greatly ruined?

Second, it loses one's standing. Among men, the worthy and the base, the high and the low, are each different. In the gambling house one asks only whether there is little money or much; who counts who is noble and who is base? They sit without order, and a servant is a friend; rank has no elder or younger, and a slave is quite a brother. They laugh at will and call one another at random. What propriety is there? What standing survives?

Third, it harms life. Having won, one goes in high spirits, day and night undivided. Having lost, one stakes one's life and comes again, heedless of hunger and cold. From this the essence is spent and the spirit wearied, and surely the body is harmed and life lost. Or if debts cannot be repaid and one has no face to meet the other, swallowing shame and enduring rage, one comes down with many illnesses in a chain. Schemes fail and strength is exhausted, and one stakes a single death to answer for it. The road to the City of Unjust Death — that is truly the destination of the gambling house. Is it not grievous?

Fourth, it disgraces one's ancestors. You hand over a man's gold and silver, and still he laughs at the prodigal for his folly. You ruin your family property, and he turns to sigh that the foolish son has done mischief. You cannot bring glory to your ancestors; instead you disgrace the family and ruin the household. The villagers all lay the blame on your forebears, and your grandfather and father must nurse resentment after death.

Fifth, it destroys family teaching. Gambling is of all things the easiest to lead men into, and within the family it is seen and heard at closest quarters. Ordinarily, when teaching the sons and younger brothers, one says they must learn good models. Yet on the spot they watch father and elder brother, and say they are but following the present pattern. Father gambles, brother gambles, servants gamble — what family rule can such a conjuring trick make? They gamble by day, gamble late at night, gamble in secret rooms; the fashion of the tiles even yields place to the fashion of lewdness. Family teaching is greatly ruined. It is enough to chill the heart.

Sixth, it squanders the family property. At first, in high spirits, one scatters gold like earth. At the end, in desperation, one casts away property like something dropped. Father and grandfather toiled a lifetime merely to set up the household; sons and grandsons in a moment squander it and ruin the family name. When the clothes are all pawned and only the body remains, which kin or friend will pity you? When fields and houses are all sold and debts still remain, to what corner of the world will you return? To think of this — is it not pitiable?

Seventh, it breeds trouble. Gambling all night and opening the table through the night: doors are left unbarred, and robbers often take the chance. Lamps and candles are never put out, and the house itself may be set on fire. It even comes to this, that prodigals worm their way in and set their schemes, and wicked men watch for their chance to do villainy. Fire is put out and doors knocked on, and host and guest cannot be told apart. Caps are pulled off and robes untied, and men and women pass the bounds of propriety. The trigger of calamity lies hidden there. Why do men not consider it?

Eighth, it separates flesh and blood. Scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants each attend diligently to their trade; father and mother, wife and children each bring joy to one another. This is the joy of the heavenly bonds and the common way of human feeling. Once a man enters the gambling house, it becomes a sea of bitterness. The hairpins and bracelets are pawned, and the wife swallows her voice and drinks down her resentment. Fields and houses are sold, and father and mother strain their eyes and knit their brows. He counts only on one man's swaggering, and never thinks of the whole household's sighs and complaints. Putting his hand to his heart and asking himself, how can he be at ease?

Ninth, it offends the law of the land. The prohibition of gambling is strictest in the new statutes. For the lighter offense, a hundred strokes of the rod and two months in the cangue, with pain that cuts to the skin. For the heavier, three years of penal servitude or a exile of three thousand li, parted forever from one's native place. The gentry and scholars are dismissed by statute — what face have they left? Clerks and runners are dealt with double — they must think of their persons and families. Rather than repent after the event, how much better to take heed beforehand?

Tenth, it incurs Heaven's censure. Looking through the ages, the houses that open gambling tables mostly meet with sudden calamity, and those who win money mostly come to utter poverty. It is all because they devour men's flesh and blood to fill their own belly and bowels, and gather up others' resentment and sorrow to furnish their own laughter. Therefore the ghosts and spirits nurse their wrath, and their vengeance will not be the least bit lenient. The way of Heaven loves to return; both sides come to ruin together. Looking at the whole affair, what profit is there in it?

The ten rules above are spoken with utmost urgency and feeling. I earnestly hope that people everywhere will calm their minds and think on them, suddenly awaken to great understanding, cut the matter in two with one stroke, and vow never again to dip in a finger. Then out of the den of jackals and wolves a man may turn and leap free. What blessing could be greater? Alas. The harm of gambling to men is worse than flood and fire, thief and robber, yet men cling to their delusion and will not awaken, and casting away life they follow it. Who is more pitiable? How sad, how grievous. This is why I speak of it with bitter weeping and flowing tears. He who sees this and still will not turn his head is surely the most foolish of men.

To separate has two senses: one is to press for debts owed and to extort by clerks and runners, making men sell their sons and daughters; the other is to take up private grudges and stir up trouble, inciting division between kin. Both are the height of inhumanity. Do they not know that flesh and blood are of one lineage? The heavenly nature is present in it, and the heavenly bond dwells there. Therefore a benevolent man, seeing another's flesh and blood in poverty and hardship and unable to survive, helps them with wealth and strength so that they may be safe; seeing them estranged and at odds, he reconciles and transforms them so that they may dwell in harmony. This is the essential road of cultivating the truth.

Zong Chuan heard a neighbor woman and her children weeping in each other's arms the whole night. He asked about it, and it was that her husband had fallen under a crime and she was selling herself to ransom him. Zong Chuan was shaken, and untied his purse to relieve her, so that husband and wife, mother and children were as before. At the time he was struggling to have a son. That year a son was born to him. Today his sons and grandsons flourish.

An Tingbo loved to sow discord, and had a ready tongue. Even the closest kin, once divided by him, straightway bred enmity. Li Zhongfu and his brother were harmonious, and because Tingbo stirred them they came to blows. Cai Lun and Zhang Yi were cousins who loved each other, and because they trusted Tingbo they broke off all relations. Other cases cannot be counted. Afterwards Tingbo fell into poverty and destitution, sores broke out on both his cheeks, his throat and tongue rotted, and he died shrieking, refusing all food.

When Emperor Yingzong of the Song came to the throne, he treated the palace attendants with little kindness, and many slandered and divided them before the empress dowager, until the two palaces were estranged. One day Han Qi and Ouyang Xiu were reporting business before the curtain, and the empress dowager sobbed and wept, setting out all the reasons. Han Qi said: This is probably because of illness that it is so at first. Once the illness is past, it will surely not be so. For at that time the emperor had fallen ill from fright and doubt. Ouyang Xiu added: The empress dowager served the late emperor for several decades, and her benevolent virtue is known throughout the realm. Formerly, when Wencheng was favored, the empress dowager bore it with ease. Now between mother and son, can she not be tolerant instead? Han Qi said again: The empress dowager has no children of her own. The emperor was raised in the palace from youth, and the empress is moreover his niece. Heaven arranged this son and daughter-in-law to be left to the empress dowager. How can she not cherish them herself? The empress's temper softened somewhat. Han Qi, fearing a change, then moved her with grave words, saying: We ministers are outside and cannot see His Majesty. The protection within rests wholly with the empress dowager. If His Majesty is not looked after, the empress dowager cannot decline the responsibility. The empress said in alarm: What words are these, Prime Minister? My heart is even more anxious. Those of his colleagues who heard it all broke into a sweat. Another day Han Qi saw the emperor alone and reported: Your Majesty's accession was all by the empress dowager's grace. It must not go unrequited. I beg you to attend to her with all care, and then there will be no trouble. The emperor said: I respectfully receive the teaching. Some days later Han Qi saw the emperor again. The emperor said: The empress dowager treats me with little kindness. Han Qi said: From ancient times there have been no few sage emperors and worthy kings, yet Shun alone is called greatly filial. Were all the rest unfilial? For parents to be kind and the son filial is an ordinary matter, not worth mentioning. Only where the parent is unkind and the son can still be filial is there something praiseworthy. I fear only that Your Majesty's service has not yet reached its utmost. Can parents ever be unkind? The emperor was greatly awakened. At that time the court had many troubles, and petty men divided them in a hundred ways. That the two palaces were in the end reconciled was the strength of Han Qi and the worthy men with him.

When a man has something he loves, such as fields and house property, books and curios, vessels and clothes and ornaments, he is sure to scheme to encroach upon and seize another's. How far is that from robbery? Yu Tieqiao said: Things have no beauty or ugliness; what is loved is prized. If another encroaches on what I love, how is my heart? Lu Zijin said: If at such a moment one thinks, This is what I love, being encroached upon and seized by another, then one need not fear that greed will fail to cease.

Zhang Gai had a mansion, vast and grand. Being short of funds, he pledged it to Zhang Jun for a thousand strings of cash. Zhang Jun loved it at heart and wished to encroach on it and cut it off entirely. So he richly bribed the broker and made out a deed of absolute sale. Later, when Gai was in straits and sought to redeem it, Jun brought out the deed and showed it: it was a deed of absolute sale. Gai wept and prayed to Heaven, saying: May your sons and grandsons likewise be as I am. Afterwards Zhang Jun's sons and grandsons all lost their voices and died. Now fields and houses are but things outside the body. For the sake of encroachment and deceit, a man pays for them with the sons and grandsons he loves most. How foolish is that? Let those who love to encroach take heed.

To help others do wrong, and to bring another's evil to completion, and to be unable to lead men toward good — all these are included. The Buddha said: To teach the Dharma and transform men is called the gift of Dharma, and it can cause living beings to hear the Dharma and hear the Way. By this cause and condition one gains immeasurable good reward. The Ledger of Merits and Demerits says: To teach men to do wrong is one fault for each matter; and for great matters, the fault is reckoned according to the matter. Accumulating this evil cause, one gains immeasurable evil reward. In my foolish view, to lead men toward good means that others' goodness all becomes one's own goodness, and one's own goodness grows daily purer; to help men do evil means that others' evil all becomes one's own evil, and one's own evil grows daily greater. The destination of good and evil is as far apart as heaven and earth; hence the response of calamity and blessing is as distinct as cloud and mud. Let men know which to cast off and which to follow.

Yang Kai was magistrate of Danyang, of a violent and overbearing nature. Yang Xun was his confidential secretary, fond of guessing at men's thoughts and hoping to win his favor. Though he clearly knew Kai was wrong, he dared not cross him. Whatever Kai did, he only sighed in admiration. One day in the height of summer Kai had more than forty clerks and prisoners beaten with the rod; two died. Xun still chimed in and called it fine. At night he dreamed that a god rebuked him, saying: It is you, in truth, who aid Yang Kai in his evil. You shall be punished with him. Soon after he came down with a foul disease and died. Seeing this, those who serve as confidential secretaries today may take warning.

Old Mr. Wu of Suzhou was poor and without a trade, and frequented the gates of the noble. He always urged the noble to do deeds of skillful means. If he met one of greedy and violent temper, he would strive with all his might to transform him by kindness. When he saw men doing good, he would surely praise and encourage them. His good virtue was very great and cannot be told in full. His son Congzhou passed the examinations while still young, and the old man lived to a great age.

Among the ten great vows of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, the first is to rejoice in others' merits, which means that when one sees others performing any merit, one rejoices and praises it. The sutra says: The blessing of rejoicing is like one man selling incense and another buying it; the bystanders are touched by its fragrance, and for the two men there is no diminution at all. Such is the reward of rejoicing in merit. Then those who help others do wrong may look at themselves in its mirror.

The gentleman disciplines himself with uprightness and treats others with mildness and kindness. Men of themselves both fear and love him. If he is always putting forth the edge of his authority, he may cow them for a time, but they will not cherish his virtue in their hearts. How can he stand above others?

Shi Liangzuo of Nanjing in the Ming was censor of the Western City while his home was in the Eastern City. Whenever he went in or out, he was angry that the neighbors did not rise for him, and so he seized several of them and sent them to the censor of the Eastern City for investigation and punishment. The Eastern City censor questioned them, and they answered: We common folk were all misled by Minister Ni. He said: How misled? They said: The minister was also a man of Nanjing. When he was in charge of the Ministry of War, the crowd would sometimes run and hide, and he would send men to stop them, saying: I am of the same village as you. If I cannot alight from my carriage when passing the village gate, how can I trouble you to rise? We common folk are very foolish, and thought Lord Shi was like Lord Ni, and so did not rise. We did not expect to meet his anger. The Eastern City censor laughed and released them. The minister refers to Duke Wenyi, Ni Yue. Alas, had Lord Shi heard these words he too should have felt shame within. How sad. The abuse of leaning on office and wielding power, lording it over others in pride — is it only this? There are those who use harsh statutes and severe law to poison the innocent; those who make light or heavy according to their own temper; those who let bribery set the outcome; those who use their office to repay favors and settle grudges; those who shield the wicked, dominate the markets, and cut off merchants. Though the kinds differ, all alike put forth their will and display their might, and all offend against Heaven. Yet power and influence are displayed for a single morning, while resentment and sin are brewed for another day. When the power is spent, retribution comes, and is there not one who repents too late? I would only hope that this repentant heart be put to use a little earlier — that would be excellent. Duke Kou Zhun said: He who governs with private crookedness repents when the hour passes. He who is rich and does not spend frugally repents when poor. He who does not learn a craft in youth repents when the time is past. He who does not study when he can repents when he must use it. He who speaks madly when drunk repents when sober. He who does not rest and care for himself when at ease repents when ill. This inscription is truly the great method for having few regrets. Men should keep it in mind at every hour.

To bend a man by reason, one still fears to rouse in him the mind that contends for victory, so that he stiffens and will not enter in. How much more, when one's own reason is crooked, to add insult and violence on top of it in order to prevail? Lu Zijin said: A sense of shame is in every man; who is willing to swallow insult gladly? To seek victory in such a way — the way of Heaven loves to return, and he who shames others shames himself instead.

Minister Lin Tuizhai, at the point of death, instructed his sons and grandsons, saying: You have only to learn to take the worst of it. Alas. From ancient times heroes have, simply because they could not take the worst of it, ruined many a matter. Yet from ancient times heroes have also, simply because they could bear insult and take the worst of it, accomplished many a matter. Han Xin suffered the shame beneath men's legs, taking the worst of it to the utmost. Afterwards he was given an altar and made general, and enfeoffed as King of the Three Qi, and the young men of Huaiyin were all under his command. From this we see: how do we know that the man who suffers insult will not one day be rich and noble, and that the man who insults others will not one day be insulted by others in turn? Let those who love to win consider this.

The people hold grain as their life. Moreover the farmer ploughs in spring and weeds in summer, with how much toil and hardship! The public grain tax and private debts all depend on this. How can one block the water channels to parch them, breach the dikes to flood them, or let livestock trample and eat them, so that what Heaven and Earth brought forth cannot be harvested, and men's strength is spent to no purpose? What inhumanity could be greater? Nor is this all. Those above who do not value the farming seasons and do not attend to water conservancy are also of the kind who ruin it, and they may be judged guilty by this same law.

In the dingwei year of the Kangxi reign of the Qing, Li Jia, a villager of Huguang, made his living trading cattle. Wishing his cattle fat, he would wait each time the rice was ripe and at the fourth watch drive the cattle out to graze, going as far as several li, and made this his regular practice. The land was wide and the people few, so no one could detect him. Suddenly one day he was struck dead by lightning, and on his back were written in vermilion the four characters: Driving Cattle to Harm the Crops.

Gao Bin was magistrate of Tangzhou. The soil was broad and the people few, and the fields lay waste. He came and surveyed the plains, and knew they could be farmed; what was lacking was only manpower. So he called for and enlisted refugees from both river valleys, allotted land according to the number of mouths, and increased the households by thirteen thousand three hundred, granting more than thirty-one thousand fields, until even the thorny wilds of mountain and forest were all turned into good farmland.

Xu Gui was magistrate of Danyang when a great drought came. He defied the prohibition and opened the dikes of Lake Lian to save the people's fields, and that year more than ten thousand qing were richly harvested.

Wang Ji was registrar of Longxi. The county had a pond and dike stretching for tens of li, whose profits had first been monopolized by a local strongman. Wang Ji took it all and gave it to the people, and the whole district was free from the affliction of drought.

Miao Shizhong was registrar of Ningling. The county had an ancient river, long silted and abandoned. He raised laborers to dredge and guide it, and the county's fields became rich soil. The hearts of these several lords were set on benefiting the common people. Let those who deliberately ruin such works, and those who sit watching flood and drought and make no law to remedy them, take warning from this.

Only after husband and wife do father and son exist. The way of marriage is a great matter. To break a marriage has several degrees: there are those who by a hundred schemes of slander break it before the union is made; those who obstruct it in many ways and break it at the moment of union; and those who stir up waves without wind and break it after the union is made. Do they not know that marriage is settled by Heaven, and how can man break it? If a marriage is broken by men, it was not a marriage after all. Yet though union and parting are from Heaven, to set one's mind on breaking it is to love the man [who breaks it]; and the crime is equal to murder. Alas. Why must the evildoer vainly cast away his conscience and bring great sin upon himself? As for a couple already united, sometimes the wife's family, because the son-in-law is poor, stirs up division; sometimes the elders, because the daughter-in-law is poor, believe slander and calumny. This too is a thief's love that kills, worse than a drawn blade, and it must not be indulged. As for despising poverty and repudiating a pledge, or relying on strength to seize a wife — this is especially harmful to heavenly principle. If the officials, swayed by favor, give a crooked judgment, and the record they supply becomes the bill of divorce, hidden merit is greatly damaged and censure will surely be deep. This too is what those who move in the world and hold office should guard against.

Xiao Li'er of Dezhou was poor in youth and ferried boats for others. By chance he picked up ten tablets of lost gold. The boat owner said: I have a daughter; I will give her to you in marriage. The betrothal was sent. One day when the boat owner was away, the man who had lost the gold traced it to him. Li asked him to confirm it, and returned it. The boat owner had a relative who wished to take the girl for himself, and taking the chance he broke the match, saying: That man is of thin fortune; in the end he will starve to death. The boat owner then drove Li away. The kinsman had just sent the betrothal gifts when his son suddenly died. Li left and still ferried boats for others. In the heat of summer he bathed beneath Lu Bridge, and something caught his foot: it was several dozen ingots of silver. He took it and went into trade, lodging with a certain host who was none other than the family that had lost the silver before. Li did his utmost to sell off the goods for him and gained double profit. The former boat owner learned that he had grown rich and in the end gave him his daughter. She bore two sons, both of whom became honored.

Ge Dingnai of Siming, while still a licentiate, passed the shrine of the Earth God every time he went to the school. The temple keeper dreamed that the god told him: When Ge the first-place graduate passes, I must stand up. Build me a screen to shield me. The keeper did as he said, and had just gathered the workmen when he had another dream: There is no need. Scholar Ge has written a bill of divorce for another, and all his examination rank has been cut away. For a man of the village was casting off his wife and could not write, and had asked Ge to write it in his stead. Ge heard of it and greatly repented, and strove to reunite the couple. In the end he only passed the provincial list, and became a vice commissioner.

Sun Hong had once written a bill of divorce for another. A friend's father dreamed that Sun Hong would have his degree cut away for this. Hong learned of it and greatly repented, and urgently charged his friend to strive to reunite the couple. From then on he set his whole mind on completing marriages, and whenever there was a divorce he would surely reconcile and protect them with all his tact. By this hidden merit he became a vice minister, and had two sons.

Fan Yangwu, magistrate of Huai'an, had a licentiate Shi Qifen whose husband and wife were sued and by law ought to be divorced. The magistrate found a way to keep them whole. When he retired from office and returned home, he fell ill, and his grandson Ruizhi invoked the planchette spirit. When it descended, it was Shi Qifen. He wrote: Through your honor's great kindness in keeping my wife and me whole, I have four sons, all now in the school. So I came especially to thank you. And your honor's benevolent virtue should long enjoy abundant blessing; there is no need to worry. In the end he died at a ripe age, and his sons and grandsons were very prosperous.

He Yuanyi and Zhao Mingfu had settled a marriage. Then Zhao's daughter lost her sight and the family fortunes dwindled. Yuanyi changed his match and betrothed himself to the Shan family. The next year both father and son died. Zhao's daughter married the scholar Ye Weixian. Weixian passed the examinations and three times governed a great prefecture.

Zheng Shutong in childhood was betrothed to a girl of the Xia family. When he passed the examinations, the Xia girl had lost her voice from illness, and his uncles urged him to marry another. Shutong firmly refused, saying: If I do not marry this girl, where is she to go? Moreover, she was betrothed before she was mute; to cast her off now that she is mute — how could my heart bear it? In the end he married her. Later Zheng rose to be an imperial attendant, and his son in turn passed the examinations.

Yang Hong was angry that his son-in-law Yao Hong did not study, and sent him back to his own home. Yao Hong begged to take leave of his wife, and was not permitted. The daughter's resentment turned to illness, and she died. Yang Hong ordered her buried in a monk's cell. When the son-in-law came to the place of burial, the door bolt drew back of itself and the door opened of itself. When her mother heard of it, she was stricken with grief and died. More than ten years later Yang Hong came to the burial place and also died suddenly.

The family instructions of Sima Guang of the Song say: In arranging a marriage, one should first examine the son-in-law and the daughter's disposition and conduct, and what the family rules are like. Do not merely covet wealth and honor. If the son-in-law is truly worthy, though he be poor and lowly now, how do you know he will not be rich and noble another day? If he is unworthy, though he be rich and noble now, how do you know he will not be poor and lowly another day? The wife is that by which a house rises or falls. If one covets a moment's wealth and honor and marries her, then, leaning on that wealth and honor, there will be few who do not slight their husbands and treat their husbands' parents with arrogance. They develop a proud and jealous nature, and the harm they do in time — can it have any limit? It even comes to this, that a man grows rich through his wife's wealth and gains office through his wife's influence. If he has any spirit of a true man, can he be without shame? Again, the common custom loves to make light betrothals in swaddling and childhood. When the children grow up, one may be unworthy and shiftless, or have a foul disease, or be poor and starving, or follow office to a distant land; and so it comes about that pledges are cast aside and promises broken, and lawsuits and imprisonments are hastened. There are many such. Therefore a family's sons and daughters should be betrothed only after they are grown. Once the letters are exchanged and the betrothal gifts given, the marriage is completed within a few months. Thus to the end of life there are no regrets and no reversals. This is what later ages should follow.

The word gou here is the gou of the Analects phrase, gou fu yi — meaning that one need not be greatly rich; only let a man become rich, and he grows arrogant. It plainly sets out the look of a petty man suddenly grown rich, acting with reckless folly. For to be rich is to be arrogant; to be arrogant is to be extravagant; to be extravagant is to be wasteful; to be wasteful is to grasp greedily at what is unrighteous, fleecing others to fatten oneself. It must come to relying on wealth and behaving tyrannically, bullying the neighbors and slighting kin and friends, spending a thousand pieces of gold on oneself without a thought and not parting with a single hair to others. Yet a blazing fire is easily spent, and the way of Heaven detests fullness. Before the arrogance has reached others, calamity has already reached oneself. This is the one thing in ten thousand that never fails.

A rich old man of Yangxi was greedy and mean. His silver and silk, his goods and grain grew daily more abundant. Chen Dongtang urged him, saying: To heap up wealth and not scatter it must bring strange calamity. Why not perform one or two charitable deeds as a long-term plan? He would not listen. Two or three years later Dongtang said to others: This man's calamity has come. Formerly he was only greedy and stingy and contemptible; lately I hear he has grown even more reckless and overbearing, arrogant and harsh in fleecing others, stopping at nothing. Is this not hastening calamity? Before long, he was indeed killed by bandits. The ancients said: Reverence and restraint are the carriage of blessing; arrogance and meanness and pride are the trigger of calamity. He who rides the carriage of blessing is steeped in peace and rest; he who treads the trigger of calamity is suddenly overthrown. This is a bright mirror for all ages. Take heed, take heed.

The Buddha said: I have two white dharmas that can save all living beings. What are the two white dharmas? The first is shame, the second is remorse. The Master said: In conduct, have a sense of shame. The Book of Rites says: When facing hardship, do not seek to escape it improperly. Today men escape improperly, and moreover are without shame. Such a man is the lowest.

Ge Shuhan and An Lushan of the Tang were both Tang generals, and often contended in pride, neither giving way to the other. When Lushan rebelled, Shuhan was taken captive. Lushan said: You always slighted me. What will you do now? Shuhan prostrated himself and answered: Your servant has fleshly eyes and did not recognize the sage. Lushan laughed and made Shuhan Minister of Works. Afterwards he killed all the Tang generals who had surrendered, and Shuhan died in the end.

Fan Chunren of the Song once differed with Sima Guang over a matter. Later the court moved against Sima Guang's faction. Han Wei, because in his days as a councilor he had differed with Guang, escaped. Someone urged Chunren to use Wei as a precedent. Chunren said: When I formerly discussed matters at court with Junshi, to differ was permissible. To use that as ground for escaping today is not permissible. Is it better to live with a guilty heart, or to die without a guilty heart? So he was banished far away. Lu Zijin said: To escape when one ought not to escape is called improper escape, and one should deeply reproach oneself with shame. Yet there is a class of men who take it calmly as a clever stroke, and instead mock the loyal and good when they are slain, and deeply deride the men of integrity when they are put to death. Such men, though they preserve their lives improperly, have died in their hearts already. What face have they to turn toward others? There is no need to speak of the curses they earn after death. As for the petty men of the marketplace who do evil and escape punishment and disaster, they little know that Heaven is only deepening their calamity. Yet they grow accustomed and feel no shame, and do not reform their evil, until at last they cannot escape and are not even aware. Is this not pitiable?

When a kindness was not one's own doing and one falsely claims it, it is nothing but a scheme for a moment's favor. In the end the truth will out, and the man will not only feel no gratitude but will despise the false claim. When a fault was truly one's own doing and one shifts it to another, it is nothing but a scheme for a moment's relief. In the end the truth will out, and the other will not only not forgive but will hate the cunning the more. This is what is meant by the petty man who is a petty man to no purpose.

When Wang Zeng of the Song was minister, if any man asked for an appointment, he would refuse him with a stern face. Afterwards, when the man was promoted and employed, Wang Zeng would never speak a word of it to him. His sons and younger brothers said: Why not let him know? Wang Zeng said: To employ the worthy is the ruler's business. If I let him know, that is to bend to private feeling and to sell a private favor.

Once there was a man who wished to give a guest a thousand pieces of gold, but feared that if he gave it openly there would be envious ones nearby. So he put the gold in a wine jar, sealed it with mud, and sent it to him. The man opened it and found the gold, and asked the reason. He said: I do not know. This wine was bought in the market; who knows who hid it there? This is fixed destiny, and it should be my elder brother's. Why ask me?

A certain county clerk of Xingshan was skilled at deceiving people. Whenever the magistrate granted someone a favor, he would say: That was the strength of my advocacy. Or when he remitted someone's punishment, he would say: That was my work in upholding him. Every good administration he claimed as his own favor, and people all praised him for having the power to turn heaven and earth around. Later the magistrate was implicated in a matter, and the higher authorities seized the clerk as well, saying: The magistrate listened to your words. All that he did, you caused him to do. How can you decline the guilt? In the end he was beaten to death with the rod.

Wang Hua, first-place graduate of the Ming, while in office was slandered by others over another matter. Someone urged him to argue his innocence. He said: This concerns my friend of the same examination year. If I clear myself, that is to accuse my friend. In the end he did not argue. Later his son Shouren, that is Master Yangming, was in office at the capital and heard the scholars' talk buzzing over this matter, and wished to submit a memorial to argue it. The elder Wang sent a letter in haste to stop him, saying: Do you take this matter as a shame to your father? I have in truth nothing shameful. Now to attack and expose my friend without cause would instead be a great shame to me. So he stopped. Ah. To prefer to acknowledge one's own fault rather than spread a friend's wrong — is that not to surpass ordinary men ten thousandfold? Would a man like this have the fault of shifting his own errors onto others?

To shift calamity onto another is like marrying a daughter off to a man: he too is willing to take a wife. To sell evil to another is like selling goods to a man: he too is willing to buy. Such machinery is very deep, and the retribution is sure to be bitter. In the end calamity comes to oneself and evil returns to oneself. What profit is there in it?

Guo Huangzhong of the Song was magistrate of Yun'an Army. One day he went to the Qixia Palace to offer incense, and dreamed that a god told him: Your honor has graciously looked after this land, and everyone has received your gifts. Yet there is a hidden matter, and I dare not fail to tell you. Tomorrow men will come escorting cattle-butchers. Besides the nine, you should look into it. At dawn the inspection office indeed brought in nine men. Among them was a soldier who claimed to have captured them and asked for a reward. In fact the oxen had been killed by the soldier, who shifted the guilt onto the nine and then seized them hoping for reward. The magistrate questioned him once, and he confessed.

Cheng Qi of Yuezhong was a shiftless fellow. When neighbors quarreled, he would always say: If you can get me drunk with wine and pay me with money, I will go in your place and use my strength for you. When men agreed, he would go in their stead while drunk, cursing and beating savagely without limit. He could also devise wicked schemes for others; so long as there was profit, there was nothing he would not do. One day, hired by another, he went to the prefectural office to bear a punishment in his place, and was so badly wounded that he died. His body lay exposed on the road. All who saw it cursed him and laughed, saying: Evil can be sold; can life be sold too?

Mencius said: What is within must take form without. Zhuangzi said: A name is the guest of reality. How can it be bought and sold? To buy and sell a name means to scatter wealth to attract it, to set bait to entice it, to use schemes to ensnare it. We often see that from ancient times loyal ministers and filial sons, chaste wives and upright scholars, though their persons were crowned with glorious fame, were sure to meet with obstruction and depression. The reason is that fame too is a blessing, and the Creator will not give a man blessing in full; to enrich here is to stint there — such is the inevitable measure. How much worse, then, is the frustration of those who have no substance and merely buy reputation? Yu Tieqiao said: Scholars today whose writings are printed and spread yet who stumble again and again in the examinations; officials whose virtuous government is sung in the thoroughfares yet who for ten years are not transferred — is this not the reason?

Chen Xiyi of the Song warned Zhong Fang, saying: Fame is the fairest vessel of ancient and modern times, and the thing the Creator most deeply begrudges. Therefore between heaven and earth there is no perfect fame. Your fame is about to rise, and something will surely come to ruin it. In later years, indeed, because of the extravagance of his trappings and carriages, he lost his good name. If even a worthy man like Zhong Fang was undone by fame, what of the false scholars, false writers, false followers of the Way, and false men of integrity of today, who praise one another and make wide connections for influence — what will their exposure be like? We often see men of fame meet disaster more miserably than ordinary folk; so those who chase empty fame do not merely diminish their blessings. How can they not take heed? As for doing good, it too values hidden merit and solid virtue; Heaven's recompense will then be no common thing.

The Surangama Sutra says: When the mind-ground is made level, then all the lands of the world are level. For the dangers of the mind-ground are hidden within, so that others do not perceive them — spears and halberds ambushed in laughter and talk, pitfalls set in the midst of intimacy. The machinery is deep and the devices secret; mountains and rivers are not more perilous than these. To conceal and store up means to hold what cannot be broken open and what cannot be peered into. Master Liaofan said: What the Creator most abhors is nothing more than scheming; therefore Heaven's recompense to the deeply perilous is sometimes excessive. Truly so.

Li Yifu of the Tang was Vice Minister of State. In countenance he was mild and courteous, and when he spoke with people he always smiled; yet he was cunning, dangerous, envious, and cruel, skilled at casting others down. His contemporaries called him a knife in a smile. Because he was soft and yet harmed things, they also called him Li the Cat. Later he was implicated in a matter and died in exile at Suizhou, and his sons and grandsons declined.

The gentleman delights in speaking of others' good and does not cover up what they excel in. He should rather nourish and steep them, so that they reach the utmost and the finest and fulfill their talent. To thwart and suppress them, so that their spirit fails and their will is dashed and they cannot expand — this comes of a jealous heart and is the most dangerous and poisonous of things.

Mu Xiu of the Song was famed for his poetry and often traveled to the capital and Luoyang. Someone wrote his poem on the wall of the forbidden precinct, and Emperor Zhenzong saw it and admired it, and asked whose poem it was, and said: With writing like this, why do the ministers not recommend him? Ding Wei thwarted him, saying: This man's conduct does not come up to his writing. From this the emperor asked no more. To set one's mind so — that is why he had no place to die. Alas. He who thwarts others knows only how to cover up what they excel in; why does he not consider that he is losing his own virtue?

The petty man glosses over his faults and shields his wrongs, paying no regard to heavenly principle. He surely thinks himself clever. Does he know that Heaven's law is hard to escape? To shield means to cover in many ways and firmly refuse to let a thing be exposed. When a man has a disease, he urgently needs a physician. To conceal the disease and dread the doctor — few who do so escape harm for a whole lifetime. Zhu Zaian said: Shielding one's faults concerns not only oneself. All the faults committed by sons and grandsons, family members, and retainers, which I do not guard against and by which I let them grow — all these are included. As for a father whose instruction is sometimes stern, and a mother who always wishes to shield her son's evil, covering and glossing so that the father does not know — this too is a great disease of shielding faults.

Li Shuqing was an officer of the prefecture's works, and was most upright and careful. His colleague Sun Rong was a secret flatterer and a petty man. Fearing that Li would expose his faults, he instead envied and slandered him. Li could not clear himself, and died of pent-up illness. His wife, in grief and rage, hanged herself. Before long Sun Rong was struck dead by lightning, and on his ribs were written the words: Shielding his own faults, he falsely harmed a good man.

Duke Xu Wenzhen, Xu Jie of the Ming, was education commissioner in Zhejiang. There was a licentiate whose essay ended with the phrase, Yan Yuan was troubled by Confucius's loftiness. Xu Jie struck it out, writing: Fabricated. He placed him in the fourth rank, and the scholar was about to be punished with the rod. The scholar reported: Yan Yuan was troubled by Confucius's loftiness comes from the Fayan of Yangzi; it is truly not fabricated. Xu Jie rose and stood, saying: I was fortunate to pass early and have never pursued learning; I nearly punished you wrongly. He changed him to the first rank.
