For a time all admired his generous measure. Later he rose to be a Grand Secretary. Every man of blessing and virtue can surely be tolerant and does not shield his own faults. This shows it.
To study the Buddha one first puts away the mark of self; to speak of benevolence one begins with overcoming the self. Both are to break this one word, shield.

To put forth one's will and display one's might is no more than violence and willfulness. To coerce and threaten is truly to rob men by force. For example, when an official, if a man will not submit to a crime, forces him to submit; if a man will not give up his wealth, forces him to give it. Or again, when he raises a public work and sets a deadline for its completion, or presses for the collection of taxes and grain more urgently than sparks and fire. And in the houses of the rich and noble: forcing women, forcing the sale of fields and houses, relying on strength to demand debts, trusting to power to press for rent — all these are threats and coercion. Men resent it and Heaven is angered; few who do so escape retribution.

Zhang Shixun of the Song was transport commissioner of Jiangxi. He saw Wang Dan and asked for instruction. Dan said: The state's monopoly profits have reached their limit. Shixun followed his words and did not seek surplus profit, and men said Shixun understood the great principle. Xue Kui was transport commissioner of Jianghuai, and on taking leave Dan had no other words but: The people's strength in the southeast is exhausted. Kui withdrew and sighed, saying: Truly the words of a prime minister. Seeing this, what benevolent man would not be lenient and compassionate toward the people's strength? For the people's life depends on those above, and those above receive the charge to shepherd the people. How can they be without benevolence, forbearance, and mildness? Let those who hold office and administer affairs consider this.

The Records of the Han say: Shao Feng, prefect of Xuancheng, was greedy, cruel, violent, and tyrannical. One day he suddenly turned into a tiger and devoured the people of his commandery. The people called him Lord Feng, and at that he tucked in his tail and went off. The local ballad said: Do not learn from Lord Feng, who in life did not govern the people and in death devours them. This may serve as a warning to those in office who take no pity on the people.

A certain country gentleman of Huguang in the Ming had amassed a thousand pieces of gold in official earnings and sent men to redeem his ancestral property. He said to his son: The current price is already double the original value, so redeeming it is a great bargain. The son was twelve, and silently made no answer. Slowly he asked: How many years has it been sold? He said: Thirty years. He asked: How many families hold the property? He said: More than twenty. He asked: How much do the small households pay in sundry fees for acquiring property? The father said the middleman's transfer fee was about such and such. The son said: I have seen the Great Ming Code: land sold more than five years may not be redeemed. Why does Father not obey the king's law? A retainer said: To redeem ancestral property is a matter of family honor. The son said: You men do nothing but flatter. Is it not also a matter of honor for Father, having become an official, to buy fertile property elsewhere? Why must it be this land? The father said: I want to redeem it. Would the villagers dare not comply? The son said: I fear precisely that the villagers, standing in awe of your power, will be forced to let it go, and that hidden virtue will be impaired. The father said: It is good that a child should understand hidden virtue. I will now reckon and repay him all the sundry fees. The son said: The fees are a small matter. Our family finds it easy to buy land; a small household finds it hard. If a family depends on ten mu to live, and now we redeem it and tell them to buy elsewhere, they can only buy five mu. How can I bear to let half that family go hungry? I beg Father not to redeem it, but to accumulate some hidden virtue to leave to his sons and grandsons. The father was long silent and said: My son's words are indeed reasonable. Only the eighteen mu beside the graves I am set on redeeming as sacrificial land. The son again asked that it be bought outright at the current price with a deed, and not called a redemption. The father agreed. The villagers were moved by his virtue and often prayed for him at the shrine of the Fierce General. Later the son at eighteen passed the successive examinations and from a ministry post was promoted to prefect of Yanzhou. One day, riding to receive an imperial decree, he crossed a bridge, his horse stumbled, and he fell into the river. Suddenly he saw the Fierce General's hand holding him up, and he sat upright at the bridge's edge. Only then did he know it was the response to the villagers' prayers. Afterwards he lived past eighty. Ah. The deeds of coercion by rich and noble houses cannot be counted. How I wish that sons and younger brothers might extend the heart of this youth of Chu, and remonstrate tactfully in every matter and so obtain blessing. Yet I know it is hard. That country gentleman — one does not know what hidden virtue he planted to have such a son.

To unleash cruelty may be found in generals and ministers, officials and commoners alike, but in none is it worse than in the use of troops, giving free rein to slaughter and plunder. Next is the handling of lawsuits, where the innocent are recklessly ensnared. Cruelty is already intolerable; how much worse to give the heart free rein in it. Of evils manifest and great, what surpasses this? Yet he who holds the power to unleash cruelty and uses it with a heart set on saving lives — of benevolence manifest and great, nothing surpasses that either.

Huang, assistant prefect of Guangzhou in the Yuan dynasty, and his wife both fell ill and lay on separate couches. His wife dreamed that a clerk holding an official document led several soldiers carrying chains and fetters. They lifted the curtain as if to seize someone and said: Not this one. Then they came to the opposite couch, lifted the curtain, and said: This is the one. Husband and wife both started awake. The husband said: I must die. When I accepted the pacification, I killed many innocent people. Now they have all come. Within a day he died.

Zhu Zaian said: Wounding and killing is spoken of with reference to both men and creatures. For between oneself and another man, though the bodily frame differs; and between a man and a creature, though the intelligence differs — yet life is not of two kinds, and the pain is equally sharp. Only try looking into yourself: Do I crave life? Do I fear death? What is my heart like? Then men and creatures are likewise no different from me. How can one be without pity and compassion, and give free rein to cruelty and violence, wounding men and killing creatures? In my foolish view, this meaning, which speaks of both men and creatures together, accords very well with the intent of the instruction. But the sense of wounding creatures has already appeared many times in this book, and so no cases are appended.

The silkworm woman and the loom woman, with ten thousand threads and a thousand strands and boundless toil, only then complete cloth and silk. Unless there is no other way at all, how can one bear to cut and tailor it? Even when ritual cannot be set aside, one should still reduce and economize. How much more when there is no cause. As for gauze and figured silk, these should be treasured all the more. Prefect Zhao's poem on the Picture of the Silkworm Woman says: The leaves are gone before the silk is spun; her cloudy hair in disarray, her powder-streaked face grown wan. In the palace gauze and figured silk are light as cloth — how can the young lord be brought to see this picture? Duke Kou Zhun once rewarded a courtesan with damask and silk, and there is a poem: One song of pipes and strings, one bundle of damask; the beauty still thinks it light. She does not know that beneath the loom's window the weaver girl throws the shuttle how many times to make it. And again: The wind stirs her robe, her single hand she blows again and again; at the dark window the shuttle creaks through the cold. In the twelfth month the day is short and yields not a foot — how unlike a bewitching concubine's single song. Every word is cutting and apt. Extend the thought: all that might be withheld from oneself to give to the poor should be given without limit.

Zhu Wuyou's family was enormously rich. His wives and concubines all wore rare brocade, and even their socks were of silk damask. The several concubines he kept spent still more extravagantly. Later he met with sudden calamity, and the family fell into decline. When Wuyou died, his wives and concubines all wore torn socks and worn shoes, and begged a foot of cloth from others and could not get it.

Zhao Shizhou's wife, Madame Wang, after several days dead, spoke through the maidservant Laixi, saying: All my life I loved to waste silk and damask, and when washing my hair and bathing my feet I used more water than I should. The underworld judges me and beats me daily with rods. I beg you to convey my meaning to Shizhou. The whole household was moved and grieved to hear it.

Duke Fan Zhongxuan of the Song, Fan Chunren, was about to take a wife, and someone reported that the bride's family used gauze for bed curtains. The duke said: Is gauze a thing for bed curtains? Our house has always been pure and frugal; how can you throw our family rules into disorder? If you dare bring it here, I will burn it. Alas. And this was merely the house of a minister. Look through the emperors of past and present: Duke Wen of Jin did not wear a double fur; the lord of Liu Song always kept a worn jacket; the consort favored by Emperor Wen of Han did not let her robe trail on the ground; Empress Ma, the Xiaoci of the Ming, always wore a plain skirt; Emperor Wenzong of Tang once put out his sleeve to show the ministers and said: This garment has been washed three times. Emperor Taizu of Song, because of a kingfisher-feathered jacket, warned his princess, saying: In wealth and honor one must know how to cherish one's blessing. If emperors and consorts and princesses were thus sparing of their blessing, how is it that the households of ordinary scholars today vie in learning luxury and extravagance, boasting of finery and competing in beauty, with concubines in gauze and children in brocade? Do they not know that one piece of clothing is the life of a thousand silkworms? If one gives free rein to waste and destruction and spends and consumes at will, then the beginning of evil is made, and the calamity of extravagance will surely be trodden. Moreover the children who today wear patched rags and shiver with cold skin — were they not once the children of brocade and damask in former years?

The Book of Rites says: The Son of Heaven does not kill an ox without cause; a great officer does not kill a sheep without cause; a scholar does not kill a dog or pig without cause. Mencius said: Only at seventy may one eat meat. For the sage loved life and would not recklessly destroy the lives of creatures. Even when there was occasion — for sacrifice, for guests, for the aged — to hunt and take birds and beasts, it was in fact only when there was no other way, and only then were they used. He did not teach the people to seek the fare of morning and evening, to gratify the desires of the palate, and to make slaughter a daily business. The Most High in his compassion has already said that even insects, grasses, and trees must not be harmed. Yet in speaking the Dharma for the people of the world, he could not but descend a level and set out the two words, contrary to ritual, with a solemn intent of binding men not to overstep. For this is the sage's heart of having no other way. The Lankavatara Sutra says: If all people did not eat meat, there would be none to kill living beings. If people today cannot wholly give up meat, let them at least gradually and by skillful means remove the mind of killing, and learn the four abstentions of the ancients: first, not to eat what one has seen killed; second, not to eat what one has heard killed; third, not to eat what was killed for oneself; fourth, not to eat what one has killed without cause. Keeping these four abstentions, one may continue one's ordinary diet, and yet have no intent to kill living beings. As for the ox and the dog, which have merit toward the world, these especially should not be eaten. If it be so, then offenses against the rule may be somewhat fewer. Therefore I set out in full below the cases concerning the cooking and slaughter of fowl and fish, oxen, dogs, sheep, and pigs, to hand down as a model and a warning.

He Ze of the Tang was of a violent and overbearing nature, and cared only for eating and drinking. He kept chickens, dogs, geese, and ducks by the thousands, and daily cooked and killed them. He had only one son, whom he loved greatly. One day he was cooking a chicken, and the water was just boiling, when his son seemed to be snatched by something into the cauldron. They hurried to save him, but he was boiled to pieces together with the chicken.
